questions.prompt: Which lines pass the best-practices test ("could it find this by reading the code, and would it go and look?") for a project CLAUDE.md? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Run one test file: `pnpm vitest run path/to/file.test.ts`"
options.rationale: The command to check work is the most useful line.

options.text: "We use React for the frontend."
options.rationale: The agent sees this immediately in package.json.

options.text: "`src/legacy/` is still live; don't copy its patterns"
options.rationale: The code misleads here; only a person knows.

options.text: "Integration tests need DATABASE_URL; see .env.example"
options.rationale: A gotcha that costs a failed run to rediscover.

options.text: "Always write high-quality, maintainable code"
options.rationale: Vague and unverifiable.

questions.explanation: Write down what the agent can't learn from the repo or would waste time rediscovering: commands, misleading spots, decisions made outside the code, and anything corrected twice.

questions.prompt: This is a simplified version of how Claude Code decides whether to read AGENTS.md by default. What does it print?

options.text: `['CLAUDE.local.md']`
options.rationale: Any CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md, or CLAUDE.local.md on the path means AGENTS.md isn't read by default.

options.text: `['AGENTS.md', 'CLAUDE.local.md']`
options.rationale: That's the non-default claude-md-and-agents-md setting.

options.text: `['AGENTS.md']`
options.rationale: CLAUDE.local.md counts.
Something is always read when instruction files exist.

questions.explanation: The trap: adding a personal CLAUDE.local.md to an AGENTS.md project stops Claude reading the team file. Use a CLAUDE.md that imports `@AGENTS.md`, or change the Project instructions setting.

questions.prompt: Your CLAUDE.md is 450 lines: a directory tour, the full release runbook, frontend rules, backend rules, and "IMPORTANT" in a dozen places. The agent misses rules often. What's the best restructuring?

options.text: Add more IMPORTANT markers to the rules it misses.
options.rationale: The docs say emphasis mostly causes over-application; long files lose lines.

options.text: Delete the directory tour, move the runbook to a skill, move frontend and backend rules into path-scoped `.claude/rules/` files, move zero-exception rules to hooks or deny rules, and keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines.
options.rationale: Each kind of content goes to the mechanism that loads it when needed or enforces it.

options.text: Split it into five files imported with `@path`.
options.rationale: Imports organize content but don't reduce context cost; all of it still loads.

options.text: Move everything into the user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
options.rationale: Then teammates lose it, and it still loads every session.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md for facts every task needs; skills for procedures; path rules for one part of the codebase; hooks and deny rules for must-never. Shorter files get followed more reliably.

questions.prompt: What does exit code 2 from a **Stop** hook do in Claude Code?

options.text: Ends the session immediately
options.rationale: It does the opposite of letting Claude stop.

options.text: Prevents Claude from stopping and continues the conversation, with the hook's stderr as the reason
options.rationale: That's what makes a Stop hook a gate, such as "not done until tests pass."

options.text: Rolls back the last edit
options.rationale: Hooks don't undo edits.

options.text: Has no effect; only PreToolUse can block
options.rationale: Stop is one of the events exit 2 can block.

questions.explanation: Exit 2 blocks on PreToolUse (the call), Stop (finishing), and UserPromptSubmit (the prompt); on PostToolUse it can only feed stderr back to Claude. Check `stop_hook_active` to avoid loops; Claude Code also caps consecutive Stop blocks.

questions.prompt: This hooks configuration is meant to run the linter after every file edit. Why doesn't it work?

options.text: The event name is misspelled; it must be `PostToolUse`.
options.rationale: Event names are case-sensitive, and unrecognized keys are easy to miss. A shape check like the lab's catches this.

options.text: Matchers can't contain a pipe character.
options.rationale: `Edit|Write` is the documented pattern.

options.text: Command hooks must be written in JavaScript.
options.rationale: Any shell command works.

options.text: Hooks only work in user settings, not project settings.
options.rationale: Project `.claude/settings.json` hooks are shared with the repo.

questions.explanation: Validate hooks config the way you'd validate any config: JSON syntax, known event names, matcher groups with a `hooks` list, and handlers with a type and command. Then confirm with `/hooks` that it's registered.

questions.prompt: You keep pasting the same 10-step "debug a production incident" playbook into chat. It involves reading logs and dashboards but no writes. What should you build?

options.text: A skill whose description says when to use it ("investigate a production incident or alert"), with the playbook in SKILL.md
options.rationale: A procedure pasted repeatedly is the documented trigger for a skill; it loads only when relevant.

options.text: A PostToolUse hook
options.rationale: Hooks run on lifecycle events, not on demand for a procedure.

options.text: Add it to CLAUDE.md
options.rationale: It would cost context in every unrelated session.

options.text: An MCP server
options.rationale: MCP connects systems; the playbook is knowledge. A skill can use an MCP server if the logs need one.

questions.explanation: Skills hold procedures and reference material; CLAUDE.md holds what every session needs. Because this playbook has no side effects, letting Claude invoke it automatically is fine; for side-effect workflows, set `disable-model-invocation: true`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Claude Code subagents match the docs? Select all that apply.

options.text: A `tools` allowlist in the subagent's frontmatter is enforced by Claude Code.
options.rationale: Restriction by configuration, not by request.

options.text: Delegating a task to a subagent makes the answer smarter.
options.rationale: The docs say it's the same or a smaller model; you get parallelism or a fresh view, not a better answer.

options.text: Each subagent's requests count against the same usage as the main session.
options.rationale: Subagents cost tokens.

options.text: A fresh reviewer subagent hasn't seen the reasoning that produced the code.
options.rationale: That independence is the point of using one for review.

options.text: Subagents share the main conversation's context window.
options.rationale: They run in a separate window (forks start from a copy).

questions.explanation: Use subagents for isolation, enforced restriction, parallel work, and independent review. Set `model: haiku` for simple jobs to cut cost.

questions.prompt: In plan mode, what happens when Claude presents its plan?

options.text: It automatically starts editing after 30 seconds.
options.rationale: Nothing edits until you approve.

options.text: You can approve and continue in auto mode, approve with manual approval of edits, or keep planning; Ctrl+G opens the plan in your editor first.
options.rationale: That's the documented flow.

options.text: The plan is discarded unless you save it with /export.
options.rationale: Approval carries the plan into implementation.

options.text: Claude opens a pull request with the plan.
options.rationale: Plan mode is local and read-only for source files.

questions.explanation: Read the plan like a design doc (files, risks, verification, extras), edit it, and only then approve.

questions.prompt: You're running four agent sessions in parallel worktrees. Two finish with diffs that both change `api/routes.py`, and you have an hour of review time today. What's the best move?

options.text: Merge both and let git resolve the conflict.
options.rationale: A textual merge can produce code neither spec describes.

options.text: Review and merge one, then have the second session rebase onto it and rerun its checks before you review it; next time, sequence tasks that touch the same file.
options.rationale: Serializing shared-file work avoids an unchecked semantic merge; your review capacity is the real limit.

options.text: Ask a fifth agent to merge all four branches at once.
options.rationale: That creates the largest, least reviewable diff of all.

options.text: Start four more sessions to use the time while you review.
options.rationale: More streams than you can review just queues unreviewed code.

questions.explanation: Parallel agents multiply output, not review capacity. Isolate with worktrees, sequence work that shares files, and cap concurrency at what you can review.

questions.prompt: Which belong in a good task spec for an agent? Select all that apply.

options.text: Acceptance criteria with specific inputs and observable outputs
options.rationale: Each one translates into a test you can write before the code.

options.text: Non-goals, such as "no new dependencies" and "no changes to the public API"
options.rationale: Prevents scope creep and states where your ambition ends.

options.text: A definition of done the agent can run (a test file plus the full suite)
options.rationale: Lets the agent close its own loop and gives you evidence to check.

options.text: A request that the code be "robust and elegant"
options.rationale: Unverifiable; it gives the agent nothing to check.

options.text: Context the code doesn't show, such as a decision from a meeting
options.rationale: Exactly the information the agent can't find by reading.

questions.explanation: Goal, testable acceptance criteria, non-goals, context, and a runnable definition of done. The same spec becomes the reviewer's yardstick.
